args.description:
Assess container and CI/CD risk for the repository MountainlandWEB__NodeGoat-20261124T085307Z (a Node.js app, OWASP NodeGoat training app). This is the only repository available. There is NO usable sandbox (docker daemon unreachable), so you cannot build or run images — do static inspection only and say so.

Your job:
1. Find and read every Dockerfile / Containerfile / docker-compose file. Report: exact path, base image and tag (and whether it is pinned by digest), whether it runs as root, whether it uses :latest, whether it copies secrets, whether it runs npm install as root, and any other risky instruction.
2. Find and read every CI/CD workflow file (.github/workflows/*.yml, .gitlab-ci.yml, Jenkinsfile, .circleci/config.yml, azure-pipelines.yml, etc.). Report: exact path, triggers, whether third-party actions are pinned to a commit SHA or a mutable tag, whether secrets are exposed to untrusted contexts (e.g. pull_request_target), and any script that runs untrusted code.
3. Report any other deployment/infrastructure files (Procfile, app.yaml, k8s manifests, .dockerignore presence).
4. Note the Node.js version used in the container/CI versus the engines field in package.json if you can see it.

Return a structured report: each item with exact file path, exact image/action reference strings as written, and a severity judgement. Separate fact (what the file says) from inference. If no Dockerfile or no CI files exist, say that explicitly — absence is a finding too. If you cannot check something, say so.

Analyze the repository MountainlandWEB__NodeGoat-20261124T085307Z (the only repository available). This is a Node.js application (OWASP NodeGoat training app).

Your job: produce a complete inventory of what the application is made of.

Specifically:
1. List the repository's top-level files and directory structure (note anything unusual: vendored code, extra scripts, binaries, .npmrc, .yarnrc, CI config, Dockerfiles).
2. Find ALL dependency manifests and lockfiles (package.json, package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, bower.json, requirements.txt, etc.) and report their exact paths.
3. Build the SBOM and dependency graph. Report: total component count, direct vs transitive counts, and the full list of DIRECT dependencies with their declared version ranges and the resolved/locked versions.
4. Report the Node.js engine requirement and any scripts defined in package.json (especially preinstall/install/postinstall/prepare).
5. For the most notable/oldest direct dependencies, report the dependency paths for any transitive packages that look risky (e.g. old versions of express, mongoose, mongodb, lodash, ejs, etc.).

Return a structured report: exact file paths, exact package names and versions as they appear in the files, counts, and the direct dependency table. Do not speculate about vulnerabilities — that is another agent's job. Only report what you actually read from files. If a tool fails, say so explicitly.
